lessons.title: The veterinary welfare assistant
lessons.html:
A recognised welfare role

The Higher Certificate in Animal Welfare (NQF 5) prepares veterinary welfare assistants, a para-veterinary category recognised by the South African Veterinary Council (SAVC). Graduates work in animal welfare organisations such as SPCAs and community clinics, often in under-served townships and rural areas where many people cannot afford private veterinary care. The programme includes practical work at a welfare organisation.

What the role covers

  • Primary animal care under the direction of a vet: vaccination, deworming, parasite control, wound care.
  • Sterilisation campaign support: preparing animals, recovery care, record keeping.
  • Handling and restraint of dogs, cats, and also working animals such as donkeys and horses, and livestock in peri-urban areas.
  • Community education: responsible pet ownership, rabies awareness, care of working animals.
  • Kennel and cattery management: hygiene, disease control (for example parvovirus in puppies), feeding and enrichment.

Welfare assistants work within a defined scope of practice. They support the veterinarian and must not diagnose, prescribe or operate independently.

The Five Freedoms

Welfare work is often guided by the Five Freedoms, a widely used framework:

  1. Freedom from hunger and thirst.
  2. Freedom from discomfort (shelter, resting area).
  3. Freedom from pain, injury and disease.
  4. Freedom to express normal behaviour.
  5. Freedom from fear and distress.

When you assess a dog chained in a yard or a donkey pulling a cart, use the freedoms as a checklist. Is there water and shade? Are there harness wounds? Can the animal move and rest normally?

lessons.title: Law, safety and working with communities
lessons.html:
The legal framework

Welfare assistants must understand the laws behind their work:

  • Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962: defines cruelty offences such as neglect, overloading and abandonment.
  • Societies for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act 169 of 1993: governs the SPCA movement and its inspectors.
  • Veterinary and Para-Veterinary Professions Act 19 of 1982: sets the scope of practice for vets and para-vets, including welfare assistants.
  • Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984: rabies is a controlled disease and suspected cases must be reported.

Safety at work

Bites and scratches are the main risk. Approach unknown dogs side-on and slowly, read body language (raised hackles, stiff body, hard stare, growling), and use a leash, muzzle or catch pole correctly. Wear gloves when handling wounds and faeces. In rabies areas, staff should discuss pre-exposure vaccination with their employer and doctor. Any bite must be washed at once with soap and running water for several minutes and reported for medical care.

Working in communities

Welfare work succeeds when the community trusts the organisation. Good practice includes:

  • Respecting owners, even when conditions are poor; most neglect comes from lack of money or knowledge.
  • Explaining in simple language and the home language where possible.
  • Offering practical help: a kennel, a bag of food, a harness adjustment for a donkey cart.
  • Reporting cruelty cases to an inspector when education does not work.
  • Keeping accurate records of every animal treated.

Self-care

Welfare work exposes staff to suffering and euthanasia. Compassion fatigue is real. Talk to colleagues, use debriefing sessions and ask for support.

Key points

  • Veterinary welfare assistants are SAVC-recognised and work under a vet's direction.
  • The Five Freedoms give a practical checklist for assessing welfare.
  • Key laws include the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 and the SPCA Act 169 of 1993.
  • Prevent bites by reading body language and using correct restraint; wash any bite immediately.
  • Respectful community engagement and self-care keep welfare work effective.
